title: Jeremy Bentham’s preserved body still sits in a glass case at a London university

cover.alt: Jeremy Bentham’s auto-icon: his dressed skeleton with a wax head, seated on a chair in his own black clothes and broad-brimmed hat inside a display case at University College London.

body: The philosopher Jeremy Bentham, the thinker behind utilitarianism, died on 6 June 1832, aged 84, and left instructions in his will that his body be dissected, his skeleton dressed in one of his black suits and seated in a chair inside a case engraved with his name. His friend Dr Southwood Smith tried to preserve the head by drying it over sulphuric acid, but the result was so grim that a wax head, fitted with some of Bentham’s own hair, was made instead. The ‘auto-icon’ was given to University College London in 1850 and now sits by the entrance of the UCL Student Centre on Gordon Square.

events.text: Dies aged 84; his will leaves his body to Dr Southwood Smith
Smith offers the auto-icon to University College London
Moved into a new glass case at the UCL Student Centre

steps.label: The will: dissect me, keep the skeleton
Head dried over sulphuric acid: too macabre
A wax head is made, with his own hair

left.label: Myth
left.text: Bentham is wheeled into every UCL council meeting and recorded as ‘present but not voting’.

right.label: Fact
right.text: It happened once, at the provost’s final meeting in 2013. The rest is a persistent myth.

slides.detail: It was displayed in the same case for many years, but repeated student pranks led the college to lock it away.

slides.question: Why does the auto-icon have a wax head?
options: The preserved head looked too macabre
The skull was needed for science
slides.explanation: Southwood Smith’s drying method worked, but the skin darkened and shrank. A wax head fitted with some of Bentham’s own hair replaced it.

slides.alt: Jeremy Bentham’s auto-icon seated in its wooden display case at University College London in 2016.
slides.caption: The auto-icon in its old wooden case at the end of the South Cloisters, where it stood until 2020.
